title: The :has() Relational Selector
summary: Style an element based on which other elements it contains or relates to.
nestedConcepts: Style a parent from its contents

subtopics.title: The :has() relational selector
subtopics.explanation: `:has()` matches an element when a relative selector inside it finds a match. For example, `article:has(img)` selects articles that contain an image. It lets CSS respond to document structure without adding a state class, but keep the selector narrow so its condition is easy to understand.

subtopics.title: Style a parent from its contents
subtopics.explanation: A parent selector can react to a child or descendant. For example, `label:has(input:checked)` can add emphasis when its checkbox is selected. This is useful when the state already exists in the markup; application state that is not reflected in the DOM still belongs in a class or component state.

subtopics.title: Keep relational selectors readable
subtopics.explanation: Combine `:has()` with a small number of clear selectors. For example, `form:has(:invalid)` can highlight a form containing invalid input. Avoid stacking several unrelated conditions in one selector; a short class name is easier to debug when the rule represents application state rather than document structure.

subtopics.title: Check browser support
subtopics.explanation: Check support for `:has()` in the browsers your users rely on. If an older browser lacks it, the core page should remain usable without the enhancement. Test the fallback in a real browser; a selector that silently stops matching can remove visual feedback even when the rest of the page loads.

subtopics.title: Prefer classes for application state
subtopics.explanation: Use a class when a style depends on application state that is not naturally expressed by the markup. For example, a saved item can receive `.is-saved` from React state. This makes the data-to-style link explicit and avoids using a complicated structural selector as a substitute for component logic.

foundations.overview: The :has() selector matches an element when its relative selector finds a match. For example, a form field wrapper can change style when it contains an invalid input. It can reduce markup-specific JavaScript, but selector complexity still deserves care.
foundations.mentalModel: It is like choosing a folder based on the items stored inside it.
foundations.whyItMatters: It lets CSS respond to relationships in the document structure.

keyTakeaways: :has() checks for a matching relative selector.
It can style a parent based on a child.
Combine it with simple selectors for readability.
Test browser support for your audience.
Use classes when application state is clearer than structure.
